## Overview

This is the second part of two for practicing calculating measures of community diversity. In part 1, we explored the diversity metrics for a single community, or alpha diversity. In this part 2, we will explore the diversity metrics across mutliple communities, or beta diversity.

- install.packages(c("dplyr","vegan","plotrix","ggplot2"))  # for multiple packages

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

library(dplyr)

### 1b. Read in files.
 
```{r read in data}
d = read.delim("kmd_test_set.txt", header=T)
rownames(d) <- d$Cluster

f = read.delim("kmd_test_second.txt", header=T)
```

For community ecology analyses, we ususall have two data matrixes: a primary matrix that is called a taxa table, and a secondary matrix of metadata. The primary matrix has one column for every sample, and one row for each taxon (or OTU, or as called in this dataset, cluster). 

In this script, the primary matrix is called 'd' and the secondary matrix is called 'f'. 

Some of the data manipulations require a matrix, which contains the abundance values only with no metadata. Here, we will define 'commu' as only the part of the dataframe that contains the taxa abundances. 

```{r}
comm <- d[,2:186]
```


### 1c. Explore the data. 

This is a small dataset, but in microbial ecology, it is usual to have thousands to tens of thousands of taxa. These datasets are much to large to view directly, so they have to be explored. 

Think of data exploration as a set of hypotheses that you test, in an iterative progression, with each experiment including expected results and evidence for whether you can accept or reject each hypothesis. 

What kind of object is my data? What are the dimensions of my data? What are the variable names? What is the structure of my data object? 
```{r exploring data}
class(d)
dim(d)    # 40852 211
names(d)
head(d)   # displays the first six rows of the data
str(d)    # returns a compact display of the data frame structure
```
We are using many of the same data exploration techniques as we used in the alpha diversity section, but some are different. What are some differences and why can't we use the same methods for alpha and beta diversity?
>

Some of the outputs generated when we explore large datasets like this produce screen dumps that are very large, and the larger they are, the less helpful they are for seeing the data. Here are some additional ways to explore very large dataframes. 
```{r}
d[1:5,1:7]
head(d[, grepl("^T1", colnames(d))])

comm[1:5,1:7]
head(comm[, grepl("^T1", colnames(comm))])
```

Now we can do the same kind of data exploration for the secondary matrix. 
```{r}
class(f)
dim(f)    # 185 8
names(f)
head(f)   # Display the first six rows of the data
str(f)  
```

These are some checks for deciding if the data needs cleaning. 
```{r}
any(is.na(comm))            # Are there any missing (NA) values?
sum(is.na(comm))            # How many missing values?
which(is.na(comm))          # Where are the missing values?
```

We should also check for rows with all zeros, and remove them. 
```{r}
zero.y <- which(rowSums(comm)==0)
comm.no0s <- comm[-zero.y,]

zero.x <- which(colSums(comm)==0) # none 
```


How many taxa in each domain in the data set? We can use the pipe operator %>% in dplyr to count the instances of each Domain (in this dataset, unhelpfully called Taxonomy). The output for counts by phylum are very long, so we can modify the code to (1) only plot the domain Archaea, and (2) put all phyla with less than 3 members into a category called 'Other'. 

```{r}
d %>% count(Taxonomy)
d %>% count(Taxonomy, Phylum)

table.by.Phylum <- d[d$Taxonomy=="Eukaryota",] %>% 
  group_by(Phylum) %>% 
  mutate(group_size = n()) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(Phylum = ifelse(group_size < 3, "Other", Phylum)) %>%
  count(Phylum)

table.by.Phylum
print(table.by.Phylum, n = Inf)
```

### 2. Richness & diversity calculations

Because richness and diversity are properties of single communities, and this dataset is a collection of 185 communities (variables, or columns in 'comm'), we need to make calculations across all the rows. R is very good at matrix algebra; you may want to review this topic ...

To calculate richness, first we need to convert abundance tables to presence-absence. 

```{r}
d.pa = comm.no0s
threshold = 1
for(x in 1:length(d.pa)){
 	d.pa[which(d.pa[,x]>=threshold),x] = 1
 	d.pa[which(d.pa[,x] < threshold),x] = 0
}
```

Let's explore this a bit to make sure it worked. 
```{r}
d.pa[1:8,1:7]
d.pa[40843:40850,1:7]
```

Why do you think there are mostly 1s for the lower-numbered clusters, and mostly zeros for the higher-numbered clusters?
>

Now we can use the presence/absence table to calculate observed richness. The adds the total for all the columns (variables, or sites), and then performes some exploratory analysis. 
```{r}
richness = sapply(d.pa,sum)
head(richness)
hist(richness)
summary(richness)
```

It looks there are two outlier samples with a very high observed richness. We can use which() to find it. this will return the item number (not the richness value). The second line of code subsets the total.richness vector to show the value of that index in the vector. 
```{r}
which(richness > 3000)
richness[c(29,101)] # 7532, 3694
d1 <- d[, -c(30,102)]
f1 <- f[-c(29,101),]

d.pa1 = d1[,2:184]
threshold = 1
for(x in 1:length(d.pa1)){
 	d.pa1[which(d.pa1[,x]>=threshold),x] = 1
 	d.pa1[which(d.pa1[,x] < threshold),x] = 0
}

richness = sapply(d.pa1,sum)
head(richness)
hist(richness)
summary(richness)
```

This line adds the calculation to the secondary matrix. This is so we can use the data on the samples (variables, or sites) to peform statistics. 
```{r}
rownames(f1) <- f1$ID
f1$richness <- richness[rownames(f1)]
head(f1)
```

Now that we have observed richness calculated for all the sites, we can perform statistics on richness. In this case we want to know if richness varies by site, and if it varies by site if we separate soil samples "Soil" from litter samples "Litt".
```{r}
summary(aov(richness ~ site, data=f1)) # n.s.
summary(aov(richness ~ site, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",])) # p = 0.0386 *
summary(aov(richness ~ site, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",])) # n.s.
```

Because there was a difference in total richness by soil type, we will keep them separate and explore if there is a variation in richness over time ("T"). This treats time as a discreet variable, but in some cases it will make more sense to treat time as a continuous variable. 
```{r}
summary(aov(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",])) # ***
summary(aov(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",])) # ***
TukeyHSD(aov(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",]))
TukeyHSD(aov(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",]))
```

By adding the taxa metadata to the presence absence matrix, we can analyze subsets of the data by taxonomy. In this example, we will examine richness by domain. We'll combine the two dataframes using cbind, but this is risky unless you are VERY SURE that your rows have not changed order. Merge is a better way to combine the dataframe based on the column with names they both share. The first line makes the column 'Cluster', so that the merge on the second line will combine them. However, merge() is slow for a big dataset like this (especially on my laptop), so we'll use cbind(). 
```{r}
d.pa1$Cluster <- rownames(d.pa1)
d.pa2 <- cbind(d.pa1, d1[,185:209])
#d.pa2 <- merge(d.pa1, d1[,185:209])

summary(aov(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",])) # ***
summary(aov(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",])) # ***
TukeyHSD(aov(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",]))
TukeyHSD(aov(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",]))
```

Now we can measure the other metrics of diversity and add them to the secondary matrix. 
```{r}
div.b <- t(d1[d1$Taxonomy=="Bacteria",2:184])

Chao.b <- t(estimateR(div.b))
H.b <- diversity(div.b, index="shannon") # Shannon's diversity; other measures are available, like simpsons and inverse simpsons
J.b <- H.b/log(specnumber(div.b)) # Pielou's J evenness index
f2 <- cbind(f1, Chao.b, H.b, J.b)
```

Now we'll make a plot of richness. This uses base R. 
```{r}
boxplot(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",], ylab="Richness (number of taxa)",
	boxwex=0.3, at=1:6 - 0.2, col="grey50", ylim=c(0,3250))
boxplot(richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",], 
	boxwex=0.3, at=1:6 + 0.2, add=TRUE)
legend(0.5,3000,c("Soil","Litter"), fill=c("grey50","white"))
```

Here is a different way to plot, using a package called lattice, which was a popular alternative to base R for plotting before ggplot took over. Here I'll switch to plotting S.chao1 instead of (observed) richness. 
```{r}
t.test(richness ~ type, data=f2) # . p = 0.0832
t.test(S.chao1 ~ type, data=f2) # ** p = 0.0075

y = tapply(f2$S.chao1, f2$type, mean) # Litt 232.266, Soil 213.143
yci = tapply(f2$S.chao1, f2$type, sd) # sd Litt 59.3, Soil 52.6

stripchart(S.chao1 ~ type, data=f2, method="jitter", vertical=TRUE, pch=21,
	ylab="Chao1 Estimated Richness", xlim=c(0.5,2.5), ylim=c(0,8000))
text(1,y[1],"_________", cex=2)
text(2,y[2],"_________", cex=2)
plotCI(c(1,2), y, yci, add=TRUE, pch=NA, scol="grey10", sfrac=0.08)
text(1.5,2500,"P=0.008")
```

And another way to plot using ggplot. 
```{r}
ggplot(f2, aes(x = T, y = S.obs, fill = type)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Richness by Site and Sample Type",
       x = "Site",
       y = "Richness (observed)",
       fill = "sample") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 3. Ordination using NMDS & plotting

Now we can start performing our ordination to see trends in the data. Ordination is a kind of multivariate statistics, where the method finds the plane through the data (defined as axis 1 and axis 2) that explain the most variation. This is akin to finding a regression line in two dimensions, but here we're looking through as many dimensions as we have taxa: in this case, 40,852 dimensions. 

Let's remove the singletons. These don't add much to the ordination, and make the calculations take extra time. 
```{r}
ones <- which(rowSums(comm.no0s) < 2)
d.no1s = d1[-ones,]
dim(d.no1s) # 18464 209
comm.no1s = as.data.frame(t(d.no1s[,2:184]))
```

Multidimensional scaling is a non-parametric method of fitting an ordination to community data. This can be a bit slow, so while this is running you can read the documentatoin on metaMDS in R. 
```{r}
mds = metaMDS(comm.no1s, distance="bray", wascores=FALSE)
mds # 2 dimensions and 0.165 stress, very good solution
plot(mds, type="t")
```

If you explore the results, which are contained in the object 'mds', you will find that this is an object with mamy objects, which R calls a list. We can call the part of the list with the coordinates for MDS1 and MDS2 using mds$points. 
```{r}
str(mds)
ID <- rownames(mds$points)
f3 = cbind(f2, as.data.frame(mds$points))
names(f3)
head(f3)
```

Once the solution is extracted, you use any plotting function you want to visualize your results. Here is a solution using dplyr (to calculate the means and standard errors by group) and ggplot. 
```{r}
# Summarize means and confidence intervals
summary_df <- f3 %>%
  group_by(site, T, type, time) %>%
  summarise(
    x_mean = mean(MDS1),
    x_se = sd(MDS1) / sqrt(n()),
    y_mean = mean(MDS2),
    y_se = sd(MDS2) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    x_lower = x_mean - 1.96 * x_se,
    x_upper = x_mean + 1.96 * x_se,
    y_lower = y_mean - 1.96 * y_se,
    y_upper = y_mean + 1.96 * y_se
  )

# Plot using orientation for error bars
pch_values <- c("Litt" = 1, "Soil" = 16)  # open circle, filled circle
color_values <- c("SCF" = "blue", "Col2" = "skyblue", "BisV" = "orange", "BisR" = "red")

ggplot(summary_df, aes(x = x_mean, y = y_mean, color = site, shape = type)) +
#  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(size = time)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = y_lower, ymax = y_upper), width = 0.2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = x_lower, xmax = x_upper), height = 0.2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = pch_values) +
  scale_color_manual(values = color_values) +
  labs(title = "NMDS ordination of community with no zeros", x = "MDS1", y = "MDS2") +
  theme_minimal()

# If you use UniFrac, you can read the PCoA points files into R and
# plot in the same way. http://bmf2.colorado.edu/fastunifrac/
```

*** Challenge
Vegan has some smart ways to overlay metadata onto ordination plots. Check out these functions and maybe try one. 

  help(ordiplot)  # some better plotting funcitons for ordination 
  help(ordihull)  # spider graphs on top of ordinations
  help(envfit)    # fits environmental vectors onto ordinations


Here are some ways to look for statistical clustering of your community by groups. 

Multi response permutation procedure (mrpp) tests whether there is a significant different between two or more groups. The mrpp statistic delta is the overall weighted mean of within-group means of the pairwise dissimilarities among sampling units.

Adonis2 calculates analysis of variance using distance matrices. The default distance method is 'bray', but other methods are available. The function partitions sums of squares of a multivariate data set, and they are directly analogous to MANOVA (multivariate analysis of variance).

Analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) provides a way to test statistically whether there is a significant difference between two or more groups of sampling units. For anosim, R is zero if the grouping is completely random, one if the between group distance far outweighs the within-group distance.
```{r}
mrpp(comm.no1s, f3$type) # A=0.038, p<0.001
mrpp(comm.no1s, f3$site) # A=0.054, p<0.001

adonis2(comm.no1s ~ f3$type, method="bray") # ***
adonis2(comm.no1s ~ f3$site, method="bray") # ***

anosim.type <- anosim(comm.no1s, f3$type)
summary(anosim.type) # R=0.207 ***
anosim.site <- anosim(comm.no1s, f3$site)
summary(anosim.site) # R=0.248 *** 
```

Here are some other 

mantel() # to show difference between two sets
varpart() # with hellinger transformation


### 4. PCoA and joint plots

If your data are a 

Here is one way to perform the principle coordinates analysis, or PCoA. 
```{r}
dmat <- vegdist(comm.no1s, method = "bray")
pcoa <- cmdscale(dmat)

fit2 <- envfit(pcoa, f3[,3:8], perm=999, display="sites")
fit2
```

There are some plotting functions that come with these functions, but as before, you can extract the variables from the object 'pcoa' and use whatever plotting function you like (base, lattice, ggplot) to make your displays nice. 
```{r}
plot(pcoa)
plot(fit2, p.max=0.1, col="red")
```
